definition: How serious, well-funded, and well-documented the project is.
Where the AI actually runs and what are the dependencies.
Whether the framework ships ready-to-use chat interface components out of the box or you have to build one yourself.
Whether the framework ships ready-to-use web API components to interface with the agent, or you have to wrap one yourself.
Whether the framework can handle many users running agents at the same time without breaking down.
Whether the framework ships a session store to persist conversations messages and state.
How the framework manages the agent loop, interacts with models and tools, and exposes messages and events.
How much control the framework gives over what the AI sees each turn, which drives both answer quality and cost.
Whether the AI can remember things about each user across conversations and tap into your company's knowledge base.
Whether you can extend the agent with packaged capabilities (e.g. "expense reports", "support tickets") without rebuilding the agent each time.
Whether the agent can delegate sub-tasks to specialist child agents.
Whether prompts, skills, and tools can be versioned and rolled out to the agent like product features.
How rich the catalog of built-in AI Tools (search, send email, edit files…) and how easy it is to add your own.
Whether the framework provides guardrails to keep the AI from saying or doing things you do not want.
Whether you can see what the AI is actually doing in production, debug it, and prove it behaved correctly.
Whether the runtime can pick the tool set per tenant, scope the skill library to a tenant, and inject tenant identity into tool calls server-side rather than via LLM-provided arguments.
Whether the framework provides AI Agent evalutation and testing capabilities to measure the agent's performance and behavior.
Whether the framework provides a local sandbox and development environment to build and iterate on the agent day-to-day.
